**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my chest like a stone dropped into still water, sending ripples through me that I’d feel for years.

Words are supposed to be light, aren’t they? Just air pushed through vocal cords, shapes drawn on paper. But some stick. Some burrow. Some become part of the architecture of a person, invisible beams holding up the ceiling of their self-worth.

II.

I once read that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. That’s 16,000 chances to build or destroy, to clarify or confuse, to love or wound. We toss them around like confetti at a parade, not realizing some of them are razor blades in disguise.

*"You’ll never be good at this."*
*"Why can’t you just be normal?"*
*"I didn’t mean it like that."*

The last one is the most insidious. The backpedaling, the gaslighting, the way a single sentence can make you question your own memory. *"I was just joking."* *"You’re too sensitive."* As if sensitivity is a flaw and not a superpower, as if the depth of your feeling is something to be sanded down, smoothed over, made palatable.

III.

There’s a Japanese concept called *kotodama*—the idea that words have a soul, that speaking them into existence gives them power. Ancient Shinto priests believed names held divine energy, that to speak a thing was to summon it. Maybe that’s why we’re so afraid of silence. In the absence of words, we’re left with the raw, unfiltered truth of our own thoughts, and that’s a terrifying place to be.

I think about this when I’m lying awake at 3 a.m., the house humming with the quiet of things unsaid. The arguments we didn’t have. The apologies we swallowed. The *"I love yous"* that got lost between the couch cushions, buried under takeout menus and unpaid bills. What would happen if we dug them up? Would they still mean something, or would they crumble like old paper?

IV.

My grandmother used to say, *"A closed mouth doesn’t get fed."* She was a woman who survived the Great Depression by sheer force of will, who could stretch a single chicken into three meals and still have broth left for soup. To her, words were tools—hammers to build with, knives to cut through bullshit. She didn’t have time for pretty metaphors. *"Say what you mean,"* she’d tell me, *"and mean what you say."*

But what if what you mean is ugly? What if it’s *"I’m lonely"* or *"I don’t know how to keep going"* or *"I think I might be broken"*? Some words feel like admitting defeat. Some words feel like standing naked in a crowded room.

V.

I wrote my first poem when I was twelve. It was terrible—rhyming *"heart"* with *"art"* in the most clichéd way possible—but for the first time, I felt like I’d taken the chaos inside me and shaped it into something tangible. Words on a page were safer than words in the air. They couldn’t be interrupted. They couldn’t be dismissed with a wave of the hand. They sat there, stubborn and permanent, demanding to be seen.

That’s the magic of writing, isn’t it? The ability to slow down time, to press pause on the relentless forward march of life and say, *"Wait. Look at this. This matters."* Even if no one else ever reads it, you’ve given your thoughts a home outside your head. You’ve made them real.

VI.

Lately, I’ve been thinking about the words we don’t say. The ones that lodge in our throats like fishbones. The *"I’m sorry"* that dies on the tip of the tongue. The *"Help me"* that gets replaced with *"I’m fine."* The *"I miss you"* that turns into a like on an old Instagram photo.

We are so good at translating our truth into something digestible. We sand down the edges, soften the blow, make it easier to swallow. But what if we didn’t? What if we let our words be messy and raw and *alive*? What if we trusted that the people who matter would stay anyway?

VII.

I have a friend who sends voice notes instead of texts. At first, I found it annoying—who has time to listen to a three-minute rambling message when you could just read a sentence? But then I started to love it. Hearing her voice, the way it cracks when she’s tired or speeds up when she’s excited, the background noise of her life (a barking dog, a honking car, the clink of her coffee cup). It’s intimate in a way that text can’t be. It’s *her*, unfiltered.

Words aren’t just the things we say. They’re the spaces between them. The sighs. The laughter. The silence when someone is trying not to cry. The way a name sounds different depending on who says it.

VIII.

I used to think that the more words I had, the smarter I was. I’d hoard them like coins, dropping SAT vocabulary into casual conversation just to watch people’s eyes glaze over. But wisdom isn’t about the quantity of words—it’s about the right ones at the right time. Sometimes the most powerful thing you can say is nothing at all.

My mother, who is the opposite of my grandmother in almost every way, has a gift for silence. She’ll listen to you vent for an hour, and when you finally run out of steam, she’ll reach over and squeeze your hand. No advice. No *"I told you so."* Just presence. Just *"I’m here."*

IX.

I wonder if we’ll ever run out of words. If one day, we’ll have said everything there is to say, and the world will go quiet. Or maybe we’ll just keep inventing new ones, stitching together sounds to describe things we didn’t even know we felt. *"Saudade."* *"Hygge."* *"Mamihlapinatapei."* Words for emotions so specific they didn’t exist in other languages until someone had the courage to name them.

What would you invent a word for? The ache of a memory you can’t quite grasp? The way sunlight looks through a stranger’s hair on the subway? The quiet panic of realizing you’re exactly where you’re supposed to be, but it doesn’t feel like you thought it would?

X.

I have 100 words left. I could fill them with advice—*be kind, speak up, listen more*—but the truth is, I don’t have answers. I just have questions, and words are the lanterns I carry into the dark.

So here’s what I know:
Words can break bones.
Words can heal them.
Words can be weapons or wings.
And sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is say them out loud.

(Even when your voice shakes.)
